# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old-School Model of Toughness

When college students were asked to describe toughness, words like "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," "stoic," and "persevering" came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked first. The traditional view equates toughness with overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, and stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

Bobby Knight exemplifies this model. Over five decades, he won more than 900 games (third most all-time), reached five Final Fours, and won three NCAA championships. His 1976 Indiana team went undefeated. Knight defined toughness as "being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself." Yet his methods included hanging tampons from lockers of players he thought "soft," frequent tirades, bringing toilet paper with feces to show players what he thought of them, and choking a player at practice. His definition of toughness was founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing through obstacles, and using fear to establish authority and control.

## Tough Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting styles on two factors: responsiveness (attunement to children's needs) and demandingness (expectations and control). Low demandingness + high responsiveness = permissive (too soft). High demandingness + low responsiveness = authoritarian (too hard). Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, and punishment—"You need to do this because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." Another study found 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. The "just right" fit occurs when expectations are high *and* support is high—high demand accompanied by warmth and understanding.

## Callousness Masquerading as Toughness

The language of toughness reveals confusion: teams are called "soft," needing "hardening up," told to "show no signs of weakness." In youth sports, children do burpees and laps to "toughen them up." In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman documented frequent vomiting after workouts and insult-laden tirades, justified by parents as "necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior." Toughness has been tied to masculinity and machismo—"man up," "stop being a pussy," "There’s no crying in baseball!" The image of toughness is more The Rock or Vin Diesel than a small female of similar prowess. Yet women consistently handle pain better than men, suggesting they may have the correct definition all along.

## Consequences of the Callous View

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed signs of profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled to "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." After he complained of cramps, it took 34 minutes to get him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911—1 hour 28 minutes total. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke.

Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, has become common due to extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to "test" athletes. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, the true notion is "to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggressive behavior, higher likelihood of substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, controlling styles link to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. Even in discipline, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior in a study of over 1,200 parents. In the Israeli military, those raised in authoritarian environments coped worse with military challenges. The style creates the appearance of discipline without fostering it. One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger... I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished"—motivation to avoid punishment, not to improve.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can."

Pete Carroll, one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl, exemplifies real toughness. He encourages meditation and yoga, shifts from meetings to ring toss if players get heated. According to one star player, "He’s never negative, doesn’t scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive." Carroll believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, and bouncing back. He replaces control with autonomy, appearance with substance, rigid pushing with flexibility, fear with inner drive, insecurity with quiet confidence. Other successful coaches following this model include Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni, who told the author, "We keep it positive here." As Ken Reed summarized, "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach."

Research from Eastern Washington University (2008) on nearly 200 basketball players concluded that the keys to mental toughness "do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

## The Author's Personal Story

The author, a University of Houston runner, collapsed during the Don Bowden Mile at Cal. He had been on pace for a four-minute mile when a strange high-pitched gasp and neck tightening shattered his focus. He pulled off the track, unable to breathe. After a year of tests, allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—the vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. The American Thoracic Society cites "strong emotions" and stress as triggers. The author's old strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. To race again, he had to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the exact moment discomfort peaked. This search for what toughness really means became the book.

The four pillars: (1) Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; (2) Listen to Your Body; (3) Respond Instead of React; (4) Transcend Discomfort.
